blocks.prompt: What a Scientist Does
blocks.text: A scientist is a person who tries to find out how the world works. Scientists do not just guess. They test. First a scientist asks a question. Then they make a careful guess. This guess is called a hypothesis. Next they do a test, called an experiment, to see if the guess was right. They watch what happens and write it down. Sometimes the guess is right. Sometimes it is wrong. Being wrong is fine. A wrong answer still teaches the scientist something new. Then they try again.

a hypothesis

blocks.prompt: How a Scientist Thinks
blocks.text: A scientist is not a kind of person. It is a way of thinking, and anyone can do it. Suppose you notice that one plant on the windowsill grows taller than the same plant in a dark corner. A scientist would not just say the sunny plant is lucky. A scientist would ask a question: does more sunlight make a plant grow taller? Next comes a careful guess, called a hypothesis: yes, more light means more growth. Then comes the important part, the experiment. You grow two plants of the same kind in the same soil, with the same water, and you change only one thing. One plant gets bright light. The other gets very little. You measure both every day and write the numbers down. After two weeks the sunny plant is much taller. Your test supports your guess. But a good scientist checks again with more plants, because one lucky result is not proof. Real science is careful, slow, and honest. It is less about being smart and more about testing your ideas instead of trusting them.

blocks.prompt: Marie Curie and the Glowing Rocks
blocks.text: More than a hundred years ago, a young woman named Maria Sklodowska left Poland for Paris, because the universities in her own country would not teach women. In France she studied physics and chemistry, and she changed her name to Marie. Marie Curie became curious about a strange kind of rock that gave off invisible rays all on its own. Nobody understood where the energy came from. Marie decided to find out. Working in a cold, leaky shed, she stirred huge pots of dark, muddy ore for years, boiling it down again and again. She was hunting for the tiny bit inside that made the rays. In the end she found not one but two new elements, materials never known before. She named one polonium, after Poland, and the other radium, because it glowed. She invented a word for the rays themselves: radioactivity. Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize, the top award in science, not once but twice, the first person ever to do so. But her discovery had a hidden danger. Nobody yet knew that the rays could harm the body. Marie carried glowing test tubes in her pockets and kept them by her bed because she loved their light. Years of that invisible radiation slowly made her sick, and it led to her death. Even now, her notebooks are so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes, and anyone who wants to read them must sign a form and wear protection.

5.title: The People Who Ask Why
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Good scientists try to prove their own ideas wrong
Evidence beats opinion
A fair test changes one thing at a time
Peer review means others check your work
If nobody can repeat it, it does not count

blocks.prompt: Why Scientists Try to Prove Themselves Wrong
blocks.text: Most people, when they have an idea they like, look for reasons it is right. Scientists are trained to do the opposite. A good scientist takes a promising idea and attacks it, hunting for the one experiment that would prove it false. This sounds backward, but it is the secret engine of science. An idea that survives every honest attempt to break it is one you can start to trust. Here is why it matters. Our senses fool us easily. A stick looks bent in water. The sun seems to circle the Earth. For most of history, people trusted what seemed obvious and were often wrong. Science is a set of habits built to catch those mistakes before they spread. The first habit is evidence: do not accept a claim because a clever person said it, or because it feels true. Ask what the measurements show. The second habit is the fair test, the experiment that changes one thing at a time so you can tell what caused what. The third habit, and maybe the most important, is sharing. When a scientist thinks they have found something, they do not simply announce it. They write down exactly what they did, in enough detail that a stranger on the other side of the world can repeat it. Other scientists then try to get the same result. This checking by others is called peer review, and it is unglamorous, slow, and essential. If nobody else can reproduce your finding, it does not count, no matter how exciting it sounded. This is why science can admit it was wrong and improve, while a rumor just hardens. Ideas that once looked solid, that the Earth was the center of everything, that illness came from bad air, were overturned by better evidence, and science moved on. Being corrected is not a failure in science. It is the whole point. A scientist is not someone who knows all the answers. A scientist is someone who has agreed, in advance, to change their mind when the evidence says they must.

6.title: The People Who Ask Why
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: DNA carries the instructions for building you

Watson and Crick built the double helix model in 1953

blocks.prompt: Photograph 51: The Picture That Cracked the Code of Life
blocks.text: Inside almost every cell of your body sits a molecule that carries the full set of instructions for building you. We call it DNA. In the early 1950s, scientists knew DNA mattered, but nobody knew its shape, and shape, in chemistry, is everything. If you can see how a molecule is built, you can often work out what it does. So a quiet race began to find the structure of DNA, and the way it was won says as much about how science really works as it does about biology. At King's College London, a young chemist named Rosalind Franklin was one of the best in the world at a difficult technique called X-ray crystallography. You cannot photograph a molecule with an ordinary camera; it is far too small. Instead, you fire X-rays through it and record how they scatter. The scattered rays leave a pattern of spots and shadows, and from that pattern, with a great deal of mathematics, you can reconstruct the hidden shape that caused it. Franklin was meticulous. She spent months improving her samples and her equipment until she produced an image now known simply as Photograph 51. It showed a clean, X-shaped smear of spots, the unmistakable fingerprint of a helix, a spiral. Meanwhile, in Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick were chasing the same answer by a different route. Rather than photographing DNA, they were building models out of cardboard and wire, trying to guess a shape that fit all the known facts. What they lacked was hard evidence about the molecule's dimensions. Then Watson was shown Photograph 51, taken by Franklin, without her knowledge or permission. The image told him at once that DNA was a helix, and Franklin's careful measurements told him how wide it was and how its parts were spaced. Within weeks, Watson and Crick had their model: the now-famous double helix, two strands twisting around each other like a spiral ladder. In 1953 they published it, and it changed biology forever. Here the story grows uncomfortable. Franklin's own report was published in the same journal, but printed after theirs, which made her painstaking evidence look like a footnote that merely supported their brilliant idea. In truth, their idea leaned heavily on her work. Franklin never learned how her photograph had been used. She died of cancer in 1958, only thirty-seven years old. Four years later, Watson, Crick, and her colleague Maurice Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize. The rules do not allow the prize to be given to someone who has died, so Franklin could not have shared it. Yet for decades her name was left out of the story almost entirely, and only recently has her role been set straight. The double helix is a triumph of science: a beautiful answer, confirmed a thousand times over, that opened the door to modern medicine. But the path to it is a reminder that science is done by people, with all their ambition and unfairness. The evidence was real and the discovery was true. How that evidence was gathered, shared, and credited was a human choice, and not always a fair one.
